text:
MegaTrans is set to return to the Melbourne Convention & Exhibition Centre in September with a conference program built around the real-world pressures and opportunities reshaping Australia’s freight and logistics sector.

Reflecting an industry in transition, the program will explore the key challenges shaping the future of supply chains, from decarbonisation and automation to workforce pressures and infrastructure planning.

A standout session, Beyond Diesel: The Best Way Forward, will feature Andrew Newman, Director of Policy and Strategy at Freight Victoria, and Heather Bone, Director of Sustainability at Team Global Express. Joined by a panel of industry experts, the session will explore practical pathways beyond diesel as the sector works toward a lower-emissions future.

Innovation across the freight task will be explored in Automate All Avenues: Driving All Modes Forward, featuring Bruno Porchietto, CEO of Victoria International Container Terminal Melbourne, and Gren John Britto, Amazon Australia DSP Country Leader. Together with fellow panellists, the discussion will examine how automation is transforming operations across ports, road and beyond.

Mid-tier operators, often the backbone of the sector, will be the focus of Reinvigorating Mid-Tier Logistics, featuring Steven Ballerini, CEO of the Australasian Supply Chain & Logistics Association. The session will bring together a range of perspectives on how these businesses are under growing pressure from rising costs, tight margins and long payment terms, and how to overcome these challenges.

Strategic infrastructure planning will take centre stage in Location, Location, Location: Establishing DCs for the Future, featuring Hermione Parsons, CEO and Managing Director of the Australian Logistics Council. Alongside other industry representatives, the session will unpack the tip and tricks needed to find the right space and how to fit it out to meet the evolving needs of the sector.

Sustainability will remain a key theme throughout the program. In Greener By Design: Manufacturing Driving Sustainability Across the Supply Chain, Scott Edwards, Associate Director Sustainability at Coca-Cola Europacific Partners Australia, will join fellow panellists to explore how sustainability is being embedded across the supply chain.

Workforce challenges will also be addressed in Recruiting Right: Overcoming Staff Shortages, featuring Tony Mellick, CEO of Hi-Trans Express. Together with other industry voices, the session will focus on practical strategies to attract and retain talent in a competitive labour market.

These sessions form part of a broader conference program that brings together a diverse lineup of speakers from across the supply chain, ensuring a wide range of perspectives and real-world insights.

With more speakers and sessions to be announced, the MegaTrans 2026 program is shaping up to give businesses practical ideas, sharper insight and a clearer path forward in a fast-changing freight and logistics landscape.

title: L'aviation propre : l'impossible défi - Le Club de Mediapart
description:
Le SAF coûte deux à cinq fois plus cher que le kérosène fossile selon les marchés [12].
Autrement dit, pour fabriquer un litre d'eSAF, il faut produire quatre à cinq fois plus d'énergie électrique que ce que ce litre restituera en vol.
La NASA estime qu'il faudrait au minimum 400 Wh/kg pour l'aviation générale et 750 Wh/kg pour l'aviation régionale [24].
[3] Ulysse, « Hausse prix billets avion kérosène 2026 : +30 % », avril 2026.
[24] L'Usine Nouvelle, « Loin du mythe de l'avion tout électrique, la difficile électrification de l'aviation commerciale », 2025.
text:
Le détroit d'Ormuz est fermé depuis le 28 février 2026. Le prix du kérosène a doublé en trois mois, passant de 650 à 1 500 euros la tonne sur le marché spot européen [1]. L'Agence internationale de l'énergie a qualifié la situation de « crise énergétique la plus grave que nous ayons jamais connue » et estime les réserves européennes de kérosène à six semaines [2]. Les billets d'avion ont augmenté de 15 à 30 % sur toutes les destinations [3]. Vingt mille vols court-courriers sont supprimés chez Lufthansa d'ici octobre [4].

On pourrait croire que cette crise force l'industrie à accélérer sa transition. C'est l'inverse qui se produit. Le carburant d'aviation durable (SAF), présenté depuis vingt ans comme la solution, représente 0,8 % de la consommation mondiale en 2026 [5]. L'avion à hydrogène d'Airbus, promis pour 2035, est repoussé à 2045 [6]. L'avion électrique commercial n'existe pas et ne peut pas exister avec la physique actuelle des batteries [7]. Pendant ce temps, les émissions du transport aérien ont battu un nouveau record le 18 juillet 2025, avec 2,523 millions de tonnes de CO₂ en une seule journée [8].

J'ai consacré un livre entier à ce sujet. Dans Au-dessus des lois, je documente le fossé entre les promesses technologiques du secteur et la réalité physique, économique et politique de sa décarbonation. L'article qui suit en résume trois chapitres, actualisés par la crise de 2026.

1. Le carburant d'aviation durable : vingt ans de promesses, 0,8 % de résultat

L'IATA promettait en 2007 que les SAF représenteraient 10 % du kérosène consommé en moins d'une décennie [9]. Le chiffre de 2026 est tombé : on en est à 0,8 %. Ce n'est pas un retard mais un échec structurel que l'industrie refuse de nommer.

Le règlement européen ReFuelEU Aviation impose depuis le 1er janvier 2025 un taux d'incorporation de 2 % de SAF dans le kérosène distribué sur les aéroports européens [10]. Le mandat est censé monter à 6 % en 2030, 20 % en 2035, 70 % en 2050. Or la production mondiale de SAF atteint 2,4 millions de tonnes en 2026 [5], quand la consommation mondiale de kérosène dépasse 300 millions de tonnes. Le compte n'y est pas, et il n'y sera pas : une étude publiée dans Nature Communications en 2025 montre que seulement 24 % des capacités de production annoncées pour 2024 ont été effectivement réalisées, et que plus de 40 % des projets prévus pour 2030 risquent d'être retardés [11].

Le prix explique une partie du problème. Le SAF coûte deux à cinq fois plus cher que le kérosène fossile selon les marchés [12]. En période de crise pétrolière, cet écart se réduit légèrement en proportion, mais il reste prohibitif en valeur absolue. Les compagnies aériennes, dont les marges sont laminées par la flambée du kérosène, n'ont aucune incitation financière à incorporer volontairement du SAF au-delà du minimum réglementaire.

Willie Walsh, directeur général de l'IATA, a résumé la situation avec une franchise inhabituelle en décembre 2025 : « Si l'objectif des mandats SAF était de ralentir les progrès et d'augmenter les prix, les décideurs politiques ont réussi » [13]. La phrase est habile. Elle rejette la faute sur les régulateurs. Elle omet que l'industrie a combattu pendant vingt ans toute taxation du kérosène qui aurait pu financer la montée en puissance du SAF, et que le mécanisme CORSIA, conçu par l'IATA elle-même, désincite activement la transition en rendant la compensation carbone infiniment moins chère que le SAF [14].

L'eSAF, ou comment transformer un problème en deux problèmes

L'e-SAF (carburant de synthèse produit à partir d'hydrogène vert et de CO₂ capté) est présenté comme l'avenir du SAF. L'Allemagne impose depuis janvier 2026 un sous-mandat de 0,5 % d'eSAF dans son kérosène [15]. Le principe est séduisant : fabriquer du kérosène synthétique à partir d'électricité renouvelable et de dioxyde de carbone capté dans l'atmosphère ou à la sortie d'usines.

Le problème est le rendement. Le procédé Power-to-Liquid qui produit l'eSAF a un rendement énergétique de 20 à 25 % [16]. Autrement dit, pour fabriquer un litre d'eSAF, il faut produire quatre à cinq fois plus d'énergie électrique que ce que ce litre restituera en vol. Les trois quarts de l'électricité injectée dans le processus sont perdus en chaleur lors des étapes d'électrolyse et de synthèse. À l'échelle de l'aviation mondiale, remplacer le kérosène fossile par de l'eSAF exigerait une quantité d'électricité renouvelable supérieure à la production électrique totale actuelle de l'Union européenne.

Le coût de production reflète cette inefficacité. Selon les estimations compilées par FTI Consulting, les premières usines produisent un eSAF cinq à huit fois plus cher que le kérosène fossile. Même dans les projections les plus optimistes pour 2030, le litre d'eSAF resterait au-dessus de 1,30 euro, contre 0,60 euro le litre de kérosène avant la crise iranienne [17]. L'eSAF est une impasse arithmétique : il faudrait une quantité d'énergie renouvelable dont personne ne dispose, à un prix que personne ne peut payer, pour produire un carburant dont personne ne veut en quantité suffisante.

Ce que le SAF ne résout pas

Plus de 80 % du SAF produit aujourd'hui passe par le procédé HEFA (Hydroprocessed Esters and Fatty Acids), qui consiste à hydrogéner des huiles de cuisson usagées et des graisses animales pour en faire du kérosène [31]. C'est la filière la moins chère, mais elle a un plafond physique : le volume mondial d'huiles usagées collectables est d'environ 8 millions de tonnes par an [32]. L'aviation mondiale consomme 300 millions de tonnes de kérosène. Même en convertissant chaque goutte d'huile de friture récupérable sur la planète, on couvrirait à peine 2 à 3 % des besoins.

Cette rareté engendre un autre problème. L'Europe importe 80 % de l'huile de cuisson usagée qu'elle utilise comme biocarburant, dont 60 % en provenance de Chine [33]. Transport & Environment a documenté l'ampleur des fraudes : il est pratiquement impossible de vérifier que ces importations sont bien de l'huile usagée et non de l'huile de palme vierge requalifiée. Le SAF « durable » repose sur une filière d'approvisionnement opaque, concentrée sur un pays, et exposée à des trafics qui annulent ses bénéfices climatiques.

Troisième limite, technique cette fois : le HEFA ne peut être incorporé qu'à hauteur de 50 % dans le kérosène conventionnel. Au-delà, la teneur en composés aromatiques chute sous le seuil de 8 %, ce qui provoque le rétrécissement des joints d'étanchéité des circuits carburant et crée un risque de fuite en vol [34]. La norme internationale ASTM D7566, qui régit la certification des carburants alternatifs en aviation, plafonne donc le mélange à 50 %, ce qui signifie qu'un avion « volant au SAF » brûle en réalité au minimum la moitié de kérosène fossile.

Et même un SAF pur à 100 %, si un jour la certification le permet, ne réglerait qu'une partie du problème. Un avion propulsé par du SAF continue de voler à 10 000 mètres d'altitude. Il continue de produire des traînées de condensation, des oxydes d'azote et de la vapeur d'eau en haute troposphère. L'étude de référence de Lee et al. (2021) dans Atmospheric Environment a montré que ces effets « hors CO₂ » (traînées, cirrus artificiels, perturbation de l'ozone) représentent les deux tiers du forçage radiatif total du secteur [18]. Le SAF réduit les émissions de CO₂ sur le cycle de vie, mais il n'élimine pas ces effets d'altitude. La réduction globale de l'impact climatique plafonne autour de 50 % par rapport au kérosène fossile. C'est loin de la « neutralité carbone » que le secteur fait miroiter.

Comme je l'écris dans Au-dessus des lois : quand l'industrie aéronautique déclare que l'aviation représente « seulement 2 % » des émissions mondiales, elle ne dit qu'un tiers de la vérité.

2. L'hydrogène et l'hybridation : l'horizon qui recule

Airbus a annoncé le programme ZEROe en septembre 2020 avec trois concepts d'avion à hydrogène et une entrée en service prévue en 2035. Cinq ans plus tard, en février 2025, l'avionneur a repoussé cet objectif de cinq à dix ans [6]. Le budget du programme a été réduit de 25 % [19]. Le démonstrateur sur A380, qui devait tester en vol des systèmes de propulsion par pile à combustible, a été abandonné [19].

Les raisons invoquées sont instructives. Airbus ne dit pas que l'hydrogène est techniquement impossible. Il dit que « l'écosystème hydrogène a au moins cinq à dix ans de retard par rapport aux hypothèses de 2020 » [6]. Traduction : il n'existe pas d'infrastructure de production et de distribution d'hydrogène vert à l'échelle nécessaire pour alimenter ne serait-ce qu'une fraction de la flotte mondiale. Aujourd'hui, 99 % de l'hydrogène produit dans le monde provient du gaz naturel ou du charbon, des procédés qui émettent massivement du CO₂ [20].

L'hydrogène liquide a une densité énergétique massique excellente (33 000 Wh/kg, trois fois celle du kérosène). Mais il doit être stocké à -253 °C dans des réservoirs cryogéniques lourds et encombrants, dont le volume est quatre fois supérieur à celui des réservoirs de kérosène pour la même énergie embarquée [20]. L'architecture entière de l'avion doit être repensée. Le rayon d'action est limité à 1 500 kilomètres dans les scénarios les plus favorables, ce qui exclut les vols long-courriers, pourtant responsables de la majorité des émissions.

Et il y a un problème que personne ne mentionne dans les communiqués de presse. La combustion de l'hydrogène produit 2,6 fois plus de vapeur d'eau que celle du kérosène à énergie équivalente [21]. Un avion à hydrogène volant à haute altitude générerait potentiellement des traînées de condensation plus intenses et plus persistantes que son équivalent au kérosène. L'avion « zéro émission » pourrait aggraver l'effet réchauffant des traînées, qui représente déjà 70 % de plus que l'effet du CO₂ dans l'aviation actuelle [18].

L'hybridation : le démonstrateur et le mirage

Le démonstrateur le plus avancé en Europe est l'EcoPulse, projet conjoint de Daher, Airbus et Safran. C'est un avion TBM modifié équipé de six hélices électriques alimentées par une combinaison de turbogénérateur et de batteries. L'EcoPulse a effectué 50 vols d'essai totalisant 100 heures de vol, dont 16 heures en mode électrique [22].

Il transporte un pilote et un passager. Le chemin entre ce démonstrateur et un avion de 150 places certifié, comme je l'écris dans Au-dessus des lois, est comparable à celui qui sépare un kart d'un camion de 40 tonnes. La fonction réelle de ces annonces n'est pas de décarboner l'aviation. Elle est de créer un horizon d'attente permanent. Tant qu'un avion propre est « en cours de développement », il est politiquement difficile d'imposer des mesures de réduction du trafic.

Même dans les scénarios les plus optimistes, l'hydrogène ne pourrait contribuer qu'à 6 à 12 % de la décarbonation de l'aviation d'ici 2050 [20]. C'est l'estimation du secteur lui-même. Elle signifie que l'hydrogène ne résoudra pas le problème climatique de l'aviation, pas même en complément des SAF. Le fossé entre la trajectoire actuelle et une trajectoire compatible avec l'Accord de Paris reste béant.

3. L'avion électrique : le mur de la physique

Le kérosène contient environ 12 000 watt-heures d'énergie par kilogramme. Les meilleures batteries lithium-ion du marché en contiennent environ 300 [7]. Le rapport est de un à quarante. Même en tenant compte du meilleur rendement des moteurs électriques (qui convertissent 90 % de l'énergie en mouvement, contre 30 % pour une turbine), le kérosène fournit six à huit fois plus d'énergie utile qu'une batterie de même poids.

Un Airbus A320, dont la masse à vide avoisine 42 tonnes, emporte 24 tonnes de kérosène pour un vol de 4 000 kilomètres. Pour stocker la même énergie utile dans des batteries, il faudrait entre 150 et 200 tonnes de batteries, soit davantage que le poids total de l'avion lui-même [7]. Et un avion, contrairement à une voiture, ne peut pas fonctionner en étant lourd : chaque kilogramme supplémentaire augmente la consommation d'énergie en vol, ce qui exige davantage de batteries, qui alourdissent encore l'appareil. Les ingénieurs aéronautiques appellent ce cercle vicieux la « spirale de masse » : plus de batteries pour compenser le poids, donc plus de poids, donc plus de batteries. Aucune technologie connue n'en sort.

La densité énergétique des batteries a été multipliée par 2,5 en quinze ans, de 120 Wh/kg en 2008 à environ 300 Wh/kg aujourd'hui [7]. Il y a dix ans, on prévoyait un doublement des performances ; elles n'ont augmenté que de 20 à 30 % [23]. Pour qu'un avion régional électrique de 50 places ait un rayon d'action comparable à son équivalent à kérosène, il faudrait atteindre 1 500 à 2 000 Wh/kg. Au rythme actuel, cet objectif se situe au-delà de 2060 [7]. La NASA estime qu'il faudrait au minimum 400 Wh/kg pour l'aviation générale et 750 Wh/kg pour l'aviation régionale [24]. CATL annonce 500 Wh/kg en batteries solides, mais les batteries tout-solide à anode de lithium métallique espérées pour 2040 ne devraient pas dépasser 400 Wh/kg [23].

Les milliards du vide

Volocopter, la start-up allemande de taxis volants, a déposé le bilan le 26 décembre 2024 après avoir levé 780 millions de dollars. L'appareil n'a jamais transporté un seul passager payant. Son autonomie : 35 kilomètres. Sa consommation par passager-kilomètre : soixante-dix fois celle du RER B qu'il était censé concurrencer [25]. Lilium, autre start-up munichoise, a brûlé 1,5 milliard d'euros pour zéro passager transporté et zéro certification obtenue avant de déposer le bilan en février 2025 [26]. Le secteur des eVTOL dans son ensemble a absorbé plus de 10 milliards de dollars de capital-risque entre 2018 et 2024 pour produire, au mieux, l'équivalent fonctionnel d'un manège pour touristes.

Avec ces sommes, on aurait pu financer la rénovation complète de la ligne de train de nuit Paris-Berlin, la création de cinq nouvelles lignes de trains de nuit en Europe, ou l'extension du réseau TGV vers des villes moyennes aujourd'hui dépendantes de l'avion [27]. Des investissements qui auraient réduit des émissions réelles, dès aujourd'hui, sur des distances où le train électrique est déjà infiniment supérieur en empreinte carbone.

Le contraste avec l'automobile est éclairant. La voiture électrique a réussi parce que les contraintes sont radicalement différentes : un véhicule au sol n'a pas besoin de vaincre la gravité en permanence, les distances quotidiennes moyennes sont compatibles avec les batteries existantes, et le poids est supporté par le sol. En aviation, le poids est l'ennemi absolu, les distances sont dix à cent fois plus grandes, et l'énergie nécessaire croît de manière non linéaire avec la masse embarquée. Ce qui a fonctionné pour la voiture ne fonctionnera pas pour l'avion.

Le seul levier que l'industrie refuse

En additionnant la contribution maximale de tous les leviers technologiques disponibles (efficacité des appareils, SAF, hydrogène, électrification au sol), l'analyse de référence de Carbone 4 montre qu'il resterait encore un fossé de 30 % d'émissions à combler pour tenir une trajectoire compatible avec un réchauffement limité à 2 °C [28]. Ce fossé, aucune innovation identifiée ne peut le combler. Seule la modération du trafic le peut.

Et cette modération a une vertu rarement mentionnée : elle est le seul levier qui agisse simultanément sur la totalité de l'impact climatique de l'aviation, CO₂ et effets hors CO₂ confondus. Moins d'avions dans le ciel, c'est moins de traînées de condensation, moins de cirrus artificiels, moins de perturbation de la couche d'ozone. C'est le seul levier sans effet rebond et sans incertitude sur son efficacité.

Pendant ce temps, en 2026, alors que le kérosène flambe et que les compagnies suppriment des vols par milliers, les émissions globales du transport aérien ont dépassé leur niveau pré-Covid pour la première fois en 2025, à 195 millions de tonnes de CO₂ pour les seuls vols au départ de l'Europe [8]. Ryanair émet 50 % de plus qu'en 2019 [29]. Le trafic continue de croître de 3 % par an. L'effet rebond dévore chaque gain d'efficacité. Et 21 compagnies aériennes européennes ont renoncé, sous la pression de Bruxelles, à utiliser un « langage écologique vague » dans leur communication, aveu tacite que le greenwashing était la norme [30].

La crise iranienne a rendu visible ce que j'analyse en détail dans Au-dessus des lois : l'aviation est un secteur entièrement dépendant d'une ressource fossile en voie de raréfaction, protégé par un régime fiscal d'exception (le kérosène n'est pas taxé, les billets internationaux sont exonérés de TVA), défendu par un lobbying parmi les plus efficaces d'Europe, et incapable de se décarboner au rythme que le climat exige. Les promesses technologiques servent de paravent. Elles reculent à mesure qu'on avance. La solution n'est jamais au coin de la rue, mais l'argument fonctionne à chaque fois, parce qu'il donne aux décideurs politiques une raison de ne rien faire tout en ayant l'air d'y croire.

text:
Escenario internacional evidencia la alta dependencia del petróleo en la aviación y proyecta desafíos para el abastecimiento, abriendo espacio a soluciones basadas en producción local y fuentes renovables.

La proyección de escasez de combustible de aviación en Europa ha encendido las alertas en la industria aeronáutica, evidenciando la alta dependencia del petróleo y la vulnerabilidad de los sistemas de abastecimiento frente a escenarios geopolíticos complejos. La situación, vinculada al cierre del estrecho de Ormuz, ha generado un aumento en los precios de los combustibles y ha puesto en riesgo la continuidad de operaciones en algunas aerolíneas.

La Directora del Centro de Energía de la Universidad Católica de la Santísima Concepción (UCSC), Dra. Laura Azócar, explicó que el problema se vuelve más crítico en el caso del combustible de aviación debido a sus exigentes procesos de refinación. “Actualmente varios países europeos no cuentan con plantas con la tecnología adecuada, lo que los obliga a importar jet fuel refinado, principalmente desde países del Golfo Pérsico”, indicó. Esta dependencia ha derivado en la proyección de escasez, incremento en el valor de los pasajes e incluso cancelación de vuelos.

En este contexto, la académica subrayó que esta crisis deja en evidencia dos aspectos centrales: la urgencia de avanzar hacia la independencia energética y la necesidad de contar con capacidades propias para asegurar el suministro de insumos estratégicos.

Frente a este escenario, los combustibles sostenibles de aviación (o SAF por las siglas en inglés de “Sustainable Aviation Fuel”) surgen como una alternativa concreta. “El SAF ofrece una clara oportunidad para prepararse frente a futuros escenarios de crisis energética. Puede utilizarse en mezcla con combustibles convencionales en vuelos comerciales y, además, es carbono neutral, lo que aporta tanto en términos ambientales como en seguridad energética”, explicó la Dra. Azócar.

La especialista advirtió que, en el caso de Chile, la totalidad del combustible de aviación es actualmente importada, lo que refuerza la necesidad de diversificar las fuentes de suministro. En ese sentido, destacó el potencial del país para producir SAF a partir de materias primas locales, como aceites de fritura, biomasa lignocelulósica, proveniente de residuos forestales y agrícolas, e hidrógeno verde.

“Chile cuenta con una alta disponibilidad de estas materias primas, además de una logística ya instalada para la recolección de aceites residuales y una industria forestal consolidada que genera residuos con potencial energético”, señaló la Directora del Centro de Energía UCSC. A ello se suma el desarrollo de energías renovables, que permite proyectar la producción de hidrógeno verde como insumo clave en estos procesos.

En el ámbito regional, la Dra. Azócar destacó que el Biobío reúne condiciones favorables para impulsar esta industria, tanto por su ecosistema industrial como por la formación de capital humano especializado. “Si se cuenta con el apoyo adecuado a los proyectos de investigación y desarrollo, es posible proyectar resultados concretos en la producción de SAF a nivel nacional”, afirmó.

En este contexto, la Universidad Católica de la Santísima Concepción, a través de su Centro de Energía, desarrolla actualmente tres proyectos orientados a la producción de combustibles sostenibles de aviación. Entre ellos destaca una iniciativa en conjunto con SKY Airline, basada en el uso de aceite de camelina, que constituye el primer acuerdo academia-empresa en Chile para la producción de SAF. A ello se suma un proyecto Fondecyt enfocado en el desarrollo de una biorrefinería de aceite de camelina para la generación de SAF y otros combustibles, y un proyecto Fondef orientado a la producción de bio jet fuel rico en compuestos aromáticos a partir de lignina kraft y aceite residual, mediante un proceso integrado de co-pirólisis e hidrogenación. Estas iniciativas reflejan el avance sostenido de la Universidad en esta línea, con foco en soluciones tecnológicas basadas en materias primas renovables y disponibles a nivel local.

En línea con estos avances, la Dra. Laura Azócar recordó que Chile se ha propuesto como meta alcanzar un 50% de reemplazo de combustibles tradicionales por SAF en vuelos comerciales al año 2050, lo que refuerza la necesidad de impulsar desarrollos tecnológicos como los que hoy se están ejecutando en el país.

En ese marco, la crisis actual en Europa no solo expone una debilidad estructural del sistema energético global, sino que también evidencia la oportunidad de acelerar la implementación de estas soluciones y avanzar hacia una mayor autonomía en el abastecimiento energético de la aviación.

title: Испания начала производить авиационное топливо без нефти
description:
Именно поэтому устойчивое авиационное топливо SAF сегодня рассматривается как наиболее реалистичный путь для декарбонизации авиации.
Именно поэтому Испания делает ставку и на другое направление — использование сельскохозяйственной и лесной биомассы.
На фоне глобальных кризисов и нестабильности на нефтяных рынках собственное производство авиационного топлива становится вопросом энергетической независимости.
Испания уже входит в число стран Европы, которые делают серьёзную ставку на устойчивое авиационное топливо.
Для страны, экономика которой во многом зависит от авиасообщения и туризма, развитие собственного производства SAF постепенно превращается в стратегическую задачу национального уровня.
text:
Испания постепенно становится одним из европейских центров производства устойчивого авиационного топлива нового поколения. Речь идёт о так называемом SAF (Sustainable Aviation Fuel) — экологичном топливе для самолётов, которое позволяет сократить зависимость от нефти и уменьшить выбросы CO₂ без полной перестройки авиационной отрасли.

На фоне нестабильности мировых энергетических рынков и роста цен на традиционное топливо тема авиационной независимости становится для Европы всё более важной. Для Испании, где туризм и авиасообщение играют ключевую роль в экономике, развитие собственного производства SAF превращается не только в экологический проект, но и в вопрос стратегической безопасности.

В отличие от автомобилей, авиация до сих пор практически не может использовать электрические двигатели для дальних перелётов.

Главная проблема — батареи. Даже самые современные аккумуляторы обладают слишком низкой плотностью энергии по сравнению с авиационным керосином. Сегодня батареи обеспечивают около 200–300 ватт-часов на килограмм, тогда как традиционное топливо — более 11.000 ватт-часов на килограмм.

Это означает, что современные технологии пока не позволяют эффективно использовать электричество для средних и дальних коммерческих рейсов.

Небольшие электрические самолёты уже существуют, однако они рассчитаны на лёгкую авиацию и короткие маршруты.

Другой вариант — водородные самолёты. Airbus продолжает развивать программу ZEROe, которая должна привести к созданию первого коммерческого самолёта на водороде.

Однако здесь возникают серьёзные сложности. Водород необходимо хранить при температуре около –253 °C, что требует полностью новой инфраструктуры аэропортов и принципиально иной конструкции самолётов.

Поэтому эксперты считают, что массовое использование водорода в гражданской авиации остаётся задачей на будущее, а не решением ближайших лет.

Именно поэтому устойчивое авиационное топливо SAF сегодня рассматривается как наиболее реалистичный путь для декарбонизации авиации.

Главное преимущество SAF заключается в том, что его можно использовать уже сейчас — без замены двигателей самолётов и без перестройки существующей инфраструктуры аэропортов.

Европейский союз уже утвердил постепенное увеличение доли SAF в авиационном топливе. Согласно программе ReFuelEU Aviation, к 2030 году содержание устойчивого топлива должно достичь 6%, а к 2050 году — 70%.

Испания активно включилась в этот процесс. Компания Repsol уже выпускает SAF на промышленном комплексе в Картахене. Одновременно через дочернюю структуру Petronor в Бильбао развивается проект синтетического топлива e-SAF, которое производится с использованием возобновляемого водорода и улавливаемого CO₂.

Компания Moeve также уже поставляет SAF в несколько испанских аэропортов и строит в Уэльве крупный завод по производству биотоплива второго поколения совместно с Bio-Oils.

Сегодня основным сырьём для производства SAF являются переработанные масла, жиры и биологические отходы. Это наиболее развитая технология, однако объёмы такого сырья ограничены.

Именно поэтому Испания делает ставку и на другое направление — использование сельскохозяйственной и лесной биомассы.

Для страны с мощным аграрным сектором это особенно важно. С помощью технологии газификации и синтеза Фишера — Тропша биомассу можно превращать в авиационное топливо.

По оценкам специалистов, потенциальный объём такого производства в Испании может достигать более 517 миллионов литров SAF в год.

Основным препятствием остаётся не сама технология, а логистика. Биомассу необходимо собирать, сортировать, обрабатывать и доставлять на предприятия, что требует серьёзной инфраструктуры и больших затрат.

Поэтому специалисты предлагают развивать децентрализованную модель производства — строить заводы ближе к источникам сырья, чтобы снизить транспортные расходы.

Эксперты подчёркивают, что тема SAF выходит далеко за рамки экологии. Для Испании авиация имеет критическое значение: она обеспечивает транспортное сообщение с островами, поддерживает туристическую отрасль и международную торговлю.

На фоне глобальных кризисов и нестабильности на нефтяных рынках собственное производство авиационного топлива становится вопросом энергетической независимости.

Испания уже входит в число стран Европы, которые делают серьёзную ставку на устойчивое авиационное топливо.

Пока электрические и водородные самолёты остаются технологией будущего, именно SAF может стать главным инструментом сохранения авиации без полной зависимости от нефти и внешних поставщиков.

Для страны, экономика которой во многом зависит от авиасообщения и туризма, развитие собственного производства SAF постепенно превращается в стратегическую задачу национального уровня.

text:
In May 2026, Amsterdam introduced sweeping regulations that ban all public advertising for airlines, meat products, and fossil fuels. This move is part of the city’s broader strategy to become carbon neutral by 2050. Alongside this ambitious climate goal, the city aims to cut meat consumption by 50%. This decision mirrors the past banning of cigarette ads, considering high-carbon activities as harmful to society. While many support this step, others warn that reducing air connectivity and targeting industries like aviation could harm the economy. Critics suggest that better alternatives could achieve similar climate goals without damaging economic stability.

Amsterdam’s Climate Goals and the Advertising Ban

Amsterdam’s advertising ban is part of its commitment to combating climate change. By targeting the aviation, meat, and fossil fuel industries, the city is taking a bold stand in reducing carbon emissions. As one of Europe’s major hubs for air travel, Amsterdam’s Schiphol Airport plays a key role in global connectivity. This new regulation is bound to affect the aviation industry significantly, especially KLM, the Dutch national airline, which relies heavily on this international gateway. While this policy may advance climate objectives, critics argue it could hurt the economy by limiting access to international flights and reducing tourism.

The Economic Impact on Amsterdam’s Tourism and Aviation Sectors

Amsterdam is a prime tourist destination, attracting millions of visitors annually. With Schiphol Airport acting as a vital international hub, this new policy may lead to fewer flight options and higher costs. Reduced connectivity could have a detrimental effect on the city’s tourism industry. It could also disrupt business travel, which is essential to Amsterdam’s role as an economic powerhouse in Europe. Therefore, the city’s tourism and aviation sectors are likely to bear the brunt of this decision. As a result, Amsterdam risks losing its global status as a tourism and business destination.

While tourism has been a significant contributor to the city’s economy, the new advertising regulations could undermine that revenue stream. The aviation sector, in particular, may struggle to adapt if the policy leads to fewer advertising opportunities. This would likely result in higher airfares and fewer flight options, which could make it harder for tourists and business travelers to visit the city. This would ultimately hurt the economy by reducing tourism revenue, which is critical for local businesses.

Could Amsterdam’s Policy Be Too Harsh on the Aviation Sector?

While Amsterdam’s new regulations are seen as a progressive step towards achieving its climate goals, there is a growing concern over their potential economic repercussions. The aviation industry is vital for international trade and tourism. Reducing connectivity could lead to fewer visitors and disruptions to key businesses that rely on easy access to the city. Instead of banning airline ads, Amsterdam could explore alternative methods to reduce emissions. For instance, offering incentives for airlines to adopt more fuel-efficient aircraft or introducing carbon offset taxes could help meet environmental goals without restricting air travel.

These alternatives would allow Amsterdam to maintain its status as a global hub while still addressing the climate crisis. This approach would give airlines the flexibility to adopt sustainable practices while keeping airfares affordable and the city’s tourism sector competitive.

Alternatives to Amsterdam’s Advertising Ban

Rather than banning advertising altogether, Amsterdam could implement policies that promote sustainability in the aviation sector. Here are a few alternatives:

Incentives for Green Aviation: Offer financial support for airlines that invest in fuel-efficient aircraft or sustainable aviation fuel. This would encourage the industry to reduce its carbon footprint while maintaining air connectivity.

Carbon Offset Taxes on Flight Tickets: Instead of banning airline ads, Amsterdam could introduce a tax on flight tickets to fund carbon offset projects. This would incentivize travelers and airlines to adopt greener practices.

Promote Renewable Energy: Amsterdam could encourage businesses to transition to renewable energy sources, offering tax breaks or other incentives for those that meet sustainability criteria.

Sustainable Tourism Initiatives: Instead of limiting air travel, Amsterdam could promote eco-friendly travel options, such as electric boats and trains, to reduce the carbon impact of tourism.

By exploring these alternatives, Amsterdam could strike a balance between achieving its climate goals and protecting its economy. Such policies would support sustainable growth while ensuring that the city remains a top destination for business and leisure travelers alike.

The Impact on Amsterdam’s Economy and Air Connectivity

Amsterdam’s new advertising regulations could have serious consequences for its economy, particularly in the aviation and tourism sectors. The city is home to one of the busiest airports in Europe, Schiphol, which serves as a key hub for both business and leisure travelers. By reducing airline advertising, Amsterdam risks decreasing global connectivity, which could harm the city’s role as an international business center. This could have a ripple effect on local businesses, especially those dependent on tourism. Hotels, restaurants, and attractions could see a decline in visitors, which would hurt the economy overall.

Furthermore, limiting air connectivity could also affect Amsterdam’s freight and logistics sectors. The city’s major businesses, including multinational corporations, depend on efficient air transportation for both passengers and goods. Reducing flight options could disrupt supply chains and affect Amsterdam’s position as a European trade hub.

A Balanced Approach: Moving Forward with Climate Goals

In conclusion, Amsterdam’s bold move to ban advertising for high-carbon industries reflects the city’s commitment to fighting climate change. However, the decision may have far-reaching economic consequences, particularly for the tourism and aviation sectors. Instead of adopting extreme measures, Amsterdam could pursue alternatives that promote sustainability without harming its economy. By incentivizing greener aviation practices and supporting the transition to renewable energy, the city can remain a global hub for business and tourism while still achieving its climate goals. It is essential for policymakers to consider the broader impact of these regulations to ensure that Amsterdam can thrive economically and environmentally.

text:
President William Ruto and his French counterpart Emmanuel Macron have signed 11 bilateral agreements aimed at strengthening diplomatic, economic, infrastructural, and technological cooperation between Kenya and France.

The agreements were signed during talks held at State House, Nairobi, on Sunday, May 10, 2026, following Macron’s arrival in Kenya for the Africa Forward Summit.

Strengthening Kenya-France ties

In a statement issued via social media after the meeting, President Ruto said Kenya and France have maintained strong diplomatic relations since 1963 and continue to deepen cooperation in areas of shared strategic interest.

According to Ruto, the decision to host the Africa Forward Summit in Kenya for the first time outside a Francophone country reflects the growing relationship between Nairobi and Paris.

“Kenya and France have maintained strong diplomatic relations since 1963. We continue to deepen this partnership in areas of shared interest for the benefit of the people of both nations,” Ruto stated.

“The decision to host the Africa Forward Summit in Kenya, for the first time in a non-Francophone country, is a strong affirmation of the growing ties between our two countries. The summit marks a significant step towards a more balanced, action-oriented, and results-driven partnership.”

Key agreements signed

The 11 agreements signed between the two countries span several major sectors, including transport infrastructure, energy, agriculture, aviation, digital transformation, and the blue economy.

Among the flagship projects announced is the modernisation of the Nairobi Central Station to the Embakasi Rail Line 5 project, expected to improve urban transport connectivity within the capital.

The two governments also signed agreements on the promotion of Kenya’s premium purple tea exports, peaceful use of nuclear energy, development of the Masinga Dam project, modernisation of meteorological services, sustainable aviation fuel production, the digital transformation initiatives, expansion of container terminal capacity at Kenyan ports, and cooperation in the blue economy and the fisheries sector.

The agreements are expected to deepen French investment in Kenya while opening new opportunities in trade, infrastructure development, climate resilience, and technology.

Officials from both countries said the partnerships aim to support economic growth, job creation, and sustainable development.

Particular emphasis was placed on green energy, transport modernisation, and innovation-driven sectors that align with Kenya’s long-term economic plans.

Africa Forward Summit

Macron is in Kenya for the Africa Forward Summit, which has brought together heads of state, business leaders, investors, and policymakers to discuss Africa’s economic transformation and future global partnerships.

The summit is focusing on issues such as artificial intelligence, climate action, green industrialisation, infrastructure, youth employment, and digital innovation.

Kenya is hosting the summit as part of efforts to position Nairobi as a continental hub for diplomacy, trade, and international investment.

France remains one of Kenya’s major European partners, with cooperation spanning transport, renewable energy, education, health, urban development, and security.

French companies have also expanded operations in Kenya in sectors such as energy, infrastructure, logistics, and telecommunications.

NAIROBI, Kenya May 10 – Kenya and France have signed 11 agreements aimed at deepening cooperation across strategic sectors, following bilateral talks between President William Ruto and French President Emmanuel Macron at State House Nairobi.

President Macron is in the country for the inaugural Africa Forward Summit, which begins tomorrow at the Kenyatta International Convention Centre (KICC).

Among the key agreements signed is the rehabilitation and modernisation of the KSh12.5 billion Nairobi Commuter Rail project, which President Ruto described as a central pillar of Kenya’s urban transport modernisation programme.

The President said Nairobi Commuter Rail Line 5 will expand and upgrade key corridors linking Nairobi to satellite towns including Syokimau, Embakasi, Ruiru and Kikuyu.

“New extensions, including the Riruta-Ngong line currently under construction, will further improve connectivity across the metropolitan area,” he said.

Kenya and France also signed an agreement establishing a joint venture to develop and finance logistics and port infrastructure valued at about KSh104 billion.

Another agreement will facilitate the purchase of premium purple tea varieties and promote Kenyan speciality teas across French retail networks, creating opportunities for value addition and improved earnings for farmers.

President Ruto said the two countries also agreed to deepen cooperation in digital transformation, including digital infrastructure, digital public services, cybersecurity, data systems and artificial intelligence.

“Kenya is building a dynamic digital economy that is driving innovation, competitiveness and regional integration through flagship initiatives such as Konza Technopolis and the Digital Superhighway,” he said.

The President noted that Kenya seeks to leverage France’s expertise in nuclear technology to support the country’s target of generating 10,000 megawatts of electricity.

“Kenya is going to benefit from France’s understanding of nuclear energy,” he said.

Additional agreements signed cover cooperation in the blue economy and fisheries, financing for the raising of Masinga Dam, modernisation of Kenya’s climate and weather services, production of Sustainable Aviation Fuel, agri-food systems transformation and expansion of the Kipeto Wind Energy Development Project by an additional 100 megawatts at a cost of KSh32.5 billion.

President Ruto also said the two countries are seeking to improve air connectivity between Kenya and France to support trade, tourism and business.

“At present, limitations in frequency, capacity and routing constrain the full potential of direct air links between our two countries,” he said.

The two leaders further agreed to strengthen collaboration in digital health, laboratory systems and epidemic preparedness, including improved use of real-time data for early disease detection and response.

“This will enhance healthcare delivery and strengthen Kenya’s capacity to respond to future outbreaks,” President Ruto said.

He also welcomed growing cooperation in education and skills development, particularly in STEM and Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET).

The President said the KSh5.6 billion University of Nairobi Engineering and Science Complex project is now moving into the implementation phase.

On regional and global issues, President Ruto said Kenya and France reaffirmed their commitment to multilateralism, climate action and reform of the global financial architecture to ensure fair and predictable financing for developing countries.

“President Macron and I agreed that the Africa-France Summit must move beyond dialogue to implementation, with a clear focus on investment, innovation and partnerships that deliver measurable results,” he said.

President Ruto said hosting the Africa Forward Summit in Kenya for the first time in a non-Francophone country reflects the growing ties between Nairobi and Paris.

“Kenya is deeply honoured to host this summit, the first to be held outside France or a Francophone African country in more than five decades,” he said.

He added that the summit marks a significant shift towards a more balanced, action-oriented and results-driven partnership between Africa and France.

The President reiterated that Kenya will continue engaging with countries that support its development agenda.

“We are not looking East or West. We are looking forward,” he said.

President Macron, on his part, said France is committed to building broader partnerships and increasing French investment across Africa.

On multilateral reforms, Macron said the Africa Forward Summit will seek to accelerate reforms to the international financial architecture and push for the agenda at the G7 Summit to be hosted in France next month.

“We will try and speed up the reform of the African Financial Infrastructure with the African Development Bank,” he said.

The French President also dismissed suggestions that hosting the summit in Kenya sidelines West African nations, saying they will be represented at the meeting.

title: CORSIA Explained: How Airline Carbon Offsetting Works
description:
CORSIA stands for the Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation.
What CORSIA covers CORSIA applies to international aviation, not domestic flights.
Where sustainable aviation fuel fits Sustainable aviation fuel and lower-carbon aviation fuels can reduce an operator's CORSIA offsetting requirement when they meet the scheme's sustainability and lifecycle-emissions rules.
Why CORSIA matters for carbon project developers CORSIA eligibility can create a more valuable buyer route, especially when eligible supply is tight.
Voluntary offsetting is separate again and is used for brand, customer or net-zero claims rather than CORSIA compliance.
text:
CORSIA stands for the Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation. It is run through ICAO, the UN aviation body, and is designed to address growth in international aviation emissions that remains after operational efficiency, aircraft improvements and sustainable aviation fuel are considered.

It is not the same as the voluntary carbon market. Airlines cannot simply buy any credit and call it CORSIA compliance. They need CORSIA Eligible Emissions Units, usually shortened to EEUs, from programmes, vintages and activity types approved through ICAO's Technical Advisory Body process.

What CORSIA covers

CORSIA applies to international aviation, not domestic flights. The obligation sits with aircraft operators on routes covered by the scheme, and the final offsetting requirement depends on their reported emissions, route coverage and ICAO's growth-factor calculations.

The scheme has three broad operating stages: a pilot phase from 2021 to 2023, a first phase from 2024 to 2026, and a second phase from 2027 to 2035. Participation was voluntary in the earlier phases, with broader participation expected in the second phase subject to exemptions and state participation rules.

How the offsetting obligation is calculated

CORSIA does not offset every tonne of aviation CO2. It focuses on growth above a baseline. ICAO's post-pandemic baseline for CORSIA is tied to 85% of 2019 international aviation emissions. In practice, airlines monitor and report covered emissions, apply the relevant sector growth factor, and then use CORSIA Eligible Emissions Units to meet their cancellation obligation for the compliance period.

The result is an important distinction for developers and buyers: CORSIA demand is driven by aviation growth, covered routes and compliance rules, not by a company's broad net-zero claim. That makes CORSIA a more rule-bound buyer segment than many voluntary offset purchases.

Where sustainable aviation fuel fits

Sustainable aviation fuel and lower-carbon aviation fuels can reduce an operator's CORSIA offsetting requirement when they meet the scheme's sustainability and lifecycle-emissions rules. That means CORSIA demand is affected by more than passenger growth. Fuel uptake, route participation and policy enforcement all influence how many units airlines ultimately need.

Why CORSIA matters for carbon project developers

CORSIA eligibility can create a more valuable buyer route, especially when eligible supply is tight. But it also raises the bar. A project has to fit an approved programme and methodology scope, satisfy vintage and start-date conditions, avoid double claiming, and increasingly secure host-country authorisation with corresponding adjustment treatment for relevant vintages.

That is why a project can be excellent in voluntary-market terms and still not be CORSIA-eligible. The credit needs to fit the CORSIA rulebook, not just the buyer's impact preferences.

CORSIA versus EU ETS and voluntary offsets

Airlines may sit inside several carbon systems at once. EU ETS applies to certain aviation emissions in Europe. CORSIA applies through ICAO rules for international aviation. Voluntary offsetting is separate again and is used for brand, customer or net-zero claims rather than CORSIA compliance. The same airline may therefore buy different credit types for different purposes.

title: Beyond the silicon ceiling: how Hong Kong's AI-fueled trade boom crafts a new 'global interface'
description:
Hong Kong’s economy is writing a new narrative, one where a surge in artificial intelligence is redefining the city’s traditional role as a super-connector.
This is the precise model the government’s “patient capital,” via the Hong Kong Investment Corporation, is designed to foster.
The global AI race is not just about faster chips; it is about whose standards govern their use.
Hong Kong’s ultimate contribution to the nation is to be the laboratory where China’s industrial might and international credibility merge.
By acting as the interpreter for concrete, code, and capital, Hong Kong will not just ride the AI wave – it will channel it.
text:
Hong Kong’s economy is writing a new narrative, one where a surge in artificial intelligence is redefining the city’s traditional role as a super-connector. The 5.9 percent real GDP growth in the first quarter – the strongest performance in five years – is not merely a statistical blip. This AI trade windfall is a direct dividend of the global technology boom, supercharging the city’s logistics and signaling a permanent structural shift.

While Silicon Valley excels in coding and other global hubs focus on niche tech, this moment reveals why only the Guangdong-HK-Macao Greater Bay Area possesses an unbeatable triad: cutting-edge AI research, a complete high-end manufacturing chain, and an international financial hub. During the 15th Five-Year Plan period, Hong Kong’s strategic destiny lies in leveraging this triple strength to fulfill two critical functions: serving as the international interface for emerging industries and acting as a translation platform between national and international standards.

The EcoCeres blueprint: from lab to production line

The recent move by EcoCeres, a local sustainable aviation fuel startup, perfectly illustrates this interface. With the backing of the Hong Kong Government and Dongguan municipal authorities, the firm is migrating its front-end research and development to mass production in the mainland. It is a masterclass in utilizing Hong Kong’s green finance certification and research edge, seeding it with the manufacturing might of the GBA, and scaling it for global markets. This is the precise model the government’s “patient capital,” via the Hong Kong Investment Corporation, is designed to foster.

However, seizing the AI moment requires breaking physical and regulatory silos. The accelerated development of the Northern Metropolis, particularly the Hetao Cooperation Zone and San Tin Technopole, must not simply become a real estate project. To truly seize the opportunity, Hong Kong must curate these spaces exclusively for the AI-biology nexus, creating a “wet-lab-to-dry-code” corridor where a biotech startup can prototype a drug-discovery algorithm in Hong Kong and validate it with Shenzhen’s medical data ecosystem on the same day.

This industrial innovation is impossible without a sophisticated financial spine. The “Finance+” strategy outlined in the latest budget aims to nourish a tech enterprise from incubation to initial public offering. Yet, the deep-tech sector often suffers from a “valley of death” at the late-stage angel phase. Hong Kong should proactively utilize the upcoming Shenzhen-Hong Kong Financial Cooperation Committee meeting to engineer a “GBA Deep Tech Co-Investment Facility.” By allowing Hong Kong-registered LP funds to route capital into mainland AI hardware via a streamlined qualified foreign limited partner framework, we can weaponize capital liquidity to build the physical infrastructure AI demands.

From steel to data: rule alignment as soft power

The final, and perhaps most profound, opportunity lies outside of code and capital: it lies in standards. This is vividly demonstrated by the first-ever global use of domestic S960 high-strength steel at the Fanling Bypass footbridge. By establishing an “equivalent material” database, local academics translated mainland steel parameters into a language recognized by international engineering regulators. This saved 30 percent in costs and validated a high-end national manufacturing standard under an international common law regime. The success of the Queen Mary Hospital’s chest pain center, which slashed recovery times from 105 minutes to 53 minutes by integrating national certification standards, further proves that standard alignment saves lives.

This blueprint must now be applied to the digital realm. Hong Kong should leverage its role in the 15th Five-Year Plan to pilot a “GBA Data Compass” – a certification mechanism that defines privacy-preserving thresholds, allowing an AI model trained on Hong Kong data to seamlessly derive insights from mainland clinical records. The global AI race is not just about faster chips; it is about whose standards govern their use. Hong Kong’s ultimate contribution to the nation is to be the laboratory where China’s industrial might and international credibility merge. By acting as the interpreter for concrete, code, and capital, Hong Kong will not just ride the AI wave – it will channel it.

text:
Hanoi is preparing to introduce phased restrictions on fossil fuel-powered vehicles within the capital’s central wards as part of a low-emission zone (LEZ) initiative aimed at reducing air pollution and accelerating the transition to green transport.

Under a draft resolution submitted to the Hanoi People’s Council, which is expected to be reviewed at a special session opening on May 12, the city will gradually limit the use of gasoline-powered vehicles in areas inside Ring Road 1.

For private gasoline-powered motorcycles, excluding ride-hailing motorbikes, residents in pilot areas will be required to register online with local authorities regarding their vehicle transition plans between July 1 and October 1, 2026.

The first phase, running from July 1 to December 31, 2026, will cover the core area of Hoan Kiem Ward, including 11 major streets such as Trang Tien, Hang Khay and Le Thai To. During the pilot period, gasoline motorcycles will be restricted from operating between 6 pm and midnight on Fridays, and from 6 am to midnight on weekends. Gasoline-powered ride-hailing motorbikes are expected to be completely banned from the low-emission zone starting July 1, 2026.

The second phase, from 2027, will expand the pilot zone to include Hoan Kiem and Cua Nam wards. By 2028–2029, the entire area inside Ring Road 1—spanning nine wards —is expected to be designated a low-emission zone.

The proposal also includes stricter emissions regulations for freight vehicles. Trucks under two tons that fail to meet Level 4 emissions standards would be prohibited from entering the zone, while compliant vehicles would face peak-hour restrictions. Larger trucks would face tighter operating-hour limits or full bans.

According to Hanoi authorities, gasoline-powered motorcycles currently account for 94–97% of vehicles in the affected wards, underscoring the scale of the transition challenge. Officials have called for stronger financial incentives, tax reductions and registration fee exemptions for green vehicles, alongside expanded charging infrastructure and clearer transition policies to build public support.

To support implementation, Hanoi plans to accelerate the development of electric buses, urban railways, public bicycles and shared electric motorbikes, while installing charging stations and automated license plate recognition systems to monitor vehicle access and enforce regulations.

A potential answer could perhaps be hydrogen fuel cells. They get you something like 24 kwh/kg or more, and their weight ratio is quite acceptable. A fuel cell for an automotive weighs 250 kilos. That's nothing compared to the weight of fuel to produce the same amount of energy.

But it still leaves the question of engines. Jet engines work by expelling hot air and combustion vapor at high velocity. Can we make an electric engines with comparable fuel efficiency and thrust?

The answer is: maybe? We can compress air with compressors. Maybe even with magnetic fields? And we could heat the air with microwave radiation. You could power that off a power cell. Then we'd have an engine and a power supply that is zero emmisions. Hydrogen fuel cells are clean, with the only exhaust being water.

Flying for 10-20minutes doesn’t serve a lot of practical purposes. Like this back-pack-jets that makes rocket man fly around, seems cool but just not something you could use daily.

Air Taxis are being tested, but it’s yet to been seen if they will take off(pun intended) as they have practical problems with where they can pick you up unlike an Uber.

Possibly, I’ve not quite seen the business case for it really close though as you still need to carry the batteries and other equipment around with you which will have a hit your fuel efficiency in cruise. This would be more likely to be a thing if there were more regulations on noise and emissions at airports though.

title: Kolaborasi TRKI UNDIP Bersama PT KPI Menuju Industri Hijau Berkelas Dunia
description:
Rombongan Program Studi Teknologi Rekayasa Kimia Industri (TRKI) Sekolah Vokasi Universitas Diponegoro hadir dengan energi besar dan semangat kolaborasi luar biasa.
Fahmi Arifan, S.T., M.Eng., IPM., MM., ASEAN Eng., Dr. Heny Kusumayanti, S.T., M.T., Yusuf Ma'rifat Fajar Azis, S.T., M.T., Sri Risdhiyanti Nuswantari, S.Tr.T., M.T., Dr. (cand) Abdullah Malik Islam Filardli, S.T., M.T., Dr. (cand) Teguh Riyanto, S.T., M.T., Sri Pudjawati, S.H., Nurul Pudiastutiningtyas, S.T., Nanik Kartikasari, S.T., Wahyu Widyati, A.Md., dan Aris Darmanto.
Rombongan TRKI disambut hangat oleh jajaran manajemen KPI seperti Bapak Budi Hermawan selaku HRD & GA Director, Bapak Pradhika Rama Ulianto selaku Production & Technical Director, serta Bapak Kus Heryadi selaku General Manager Technic.
Harus ada dampak nyata, inovasi nyata, dan transformasi nyata.
Kunjungan ini membuktikan bahwa TRKI Vokasi UNDIP tidak hanya hadir sebagai program studi, tetapi telah berkembang menjadi pusat inovasi vokasi yang aktif membangun sinergi strategis bersama industri nasional.
text:
Begitu roda pesawat menyentuh landasan Bandara Sultan Aji Muhammad Sulaiman Balikpapan pada Selasa, 5 Mei 2026, suasana langsung terasa berbeda. Ini bukan sekadar kunjungan industri biasa. Ini seperti "roadshow Avengers versi teknik kimia vokasi" --- bedanya bukan menyelamatkan bumi dengan palu Thor, tetapi dengan inovasi, riset terapan, efisiensi energi, dan ide-ide industrial sustainability yang bikin ruang meeting mendadak terasa seperti forum masa depan dunia energi Indonesia.

Rombongan Program Studi Teknologi Rekayasa Kimia Industri (TRKI) Sekolah Vokasi Universitas Diponegoro hadir dengan energi besar dan semangat kolaborasi luar biasa. Dipimpin langsung oleh Kaprodi TRKI, Dr. Mohamad Endy Julianto, S.T., M.T., bersama Hermawan Dwi Ariyanto, S.T., M.Sc., Ph.D. selaku Sekretaris Program Studi, rombongan dosen dan tenaga kependidikan terbaik TRKI bergerak dari Semarang menuju Balikpapan, Bontang, hingga kawasan IKN membawa satu misi penting: menjadikan pendidikan vokasi sebagai pusat lahirnya solusi nyata industri masa depan.

Turut hadir dalam rombongan tersebut Dr. Ir. Fahmi Arifan, S.T., M.Eng., IPM., MM., ASEAN Eng., Dr. Heny Kusumayanti, S.T., M.T., Yusuf Ma'rifat Fajar Azis, S.T., M.T., Sri Risdhiyanti Nuswantari, S.Tr.T., M.T., Dr. (cand) Abdullah Malik Islam Filardli, S.T., M.T., Dr. (cand) Teguh Riyanto, S.T., M.T., Sri Pudjawati, S.H., Nurul Pudiastutiningtyas, S.T., Nanik Kartikasari, S.T., Wahyu Widyati, A.Md., dan Aris Darmanto. Kombinasi ini benar-benar seperti "dream team" vokasi UNDIP --- lengkap, solid, dan penuh semangat membangun jejaring industri nasional.

Kunjungan ke PT Kaltim Parna Industri (KPI) menjadi salah satu momen paling strategis dalam perjalanan tersebut. Perusahaan amonia raksasa yang berlokasi di Kawasan Industri Kaltim, Bontang, ini dikenal sebagai salah satu industri petrokimia nasional dengan kapasitas produksi sekitar 530.000 ton amonia per tahun dan teknologi kelas dunia berbasis Haldor Topsoe serta Mitsubishi Heavy Industries. Bahkan KPI menjadi perusahaan pertama di Indonesia yang menerapkan Closed Sea Cooling Tower sebagai bagian dari komitmen lingkungan berkelanjutan. Keren? Jelas. Tapi yang lebih keren lagi adalah ketika dunia industri bertemu dunia vokasi dalam satu frekuensi visi besar.

Rombongan TRKI disambut hangat oleh jajaran manajemen KPI seperti Bapak Budi Hermawan selaku HRD & GA Director, Bapak Pradhika Rama Ulianto selaku Production & Technical Director, serta Bapak Kus Heryadi selaku General Manager Technic. Diskusi yang terbangun terasa sangat hidup, penuh gagasan strategis, dan jauh dari suasana formal yang kaku. Yang dibahas bukan hanya soal kunjungan mahasiswa atau magang biasa, tetapi bagaimana membangun ekosistem kolaborasi jangka panjang antara kampus vokasi dan industri energi nasional.

Dalam kesempatan tersebut, Dr. Mohamad Endy Julianto menyampaikan bahwa perguruan tinggi vokasi saat ini tidak lagi hanya menjadi "pabrik lulusan", tetapi telah bergerak menjadi co-creator solusi industri. Melalui pendekatan Project-Based Learning berbasis problem solving, mahasiswa TRKI dilatih langsung menyelesaikan persoalan nyata industri mulai dari optimasi proses, efisiensi utilitas, keselamatan berbasis HSE, hingga pendekatan green industry dan circular economy.

Bahkan salah satu topik yang paling menarik perhatian adalah gagasan pemanfaatan 85% sisa buangan CO KPI menjadi peluang ekonomi baru berbasis integrated low-carbon chemical industry. Ide pengembangan green methanol, dry ice, food grade CO, microalgae, hingga sustainable aviation fuel menjadi pembahasan yang sangat visioner. Bayangkan... gas buangan yang biasanya dianggap "musuh lingkungan" justru bisa berubah jadi peluang bisnis masa depan. Ini benar-benar definisi "jangan remehkan mantan... eh maksudnya jangan remehkan CO."

Diskusi menjadi semakin menarik ketika dibahas peluang integrasi CSR industri dengan teaching factory, laboratorium terapan, sertifikasi mahasiswa, hingga riset-riset aplikatif berbasis kebutuhan industri. Semua sepakat bahwa kolaborasi kampus dan industri tidak boleh berhenti di seremoni foto bersama dan tukar plakat saja. Harus ada dampak nyata, inovasi nyata, dan transformasi nyata.

Kunjungan ini membuktikan bahwa TRKI Vokasi UNDIP tidak hanya hadir sebagai program studi, tetapi telah berkembang menjadi pusat inovasi vokasi yang aktif membangun sinergi strategis bersama industri nasional. Dari Semarang menuju Balikpapan dan Bontang, langkah ini bukan sekadar perjalanan akademik, melainkan bagian dari perjalanan besar membangun masa depan industri Indonesia yang lebih hijau, modern, adaptif, dan berdaya saing global.

Dan mungkin di situlah bagian paling "wooo" dari semuanya --- ketika dosen, tendik, industri, mahasiswa, teknologi, hingga ide-ide masa depan bertemu dalam satu meja diskusi, Indonesia sebenarnya sedang menulis bab baru tentang kebangkitan vokasi dan industri nasional.

text:
In the face of rising fuel prices, South African motorists can now enhance their car-buying strategy with new tools that reveal just how much fuel efficiency can save them annually—potentially over R7,000. Will consumers adapt their choices to secure a more economical driving future?

Image: Supplied

As fuel prices continue their relentless ascent, South Africans are finding themselves at a crossroads regarding vehicle ownership.

The latest fuel hike has prompted consumers to shift their focus from the initial purchase price of vehicles to the ever-increasing costs associated with fuel consumption and overall ownership.

This shift is underscored by a growing awareness of fuel efficiency as a critical factor in car-buying decisions.

Antoine Caradonna, managing director of VehicleSA, noted the palpable shift in consumer mindset.

"While electric vehicles are capturing interest, they remain financially out of reach for many. Buyers are now asking a more practical question: can I afford to drive this car every day?"

With everyday expenses weighing heavily on household budgets, the need for economical driving has never been more pronounced.

In response to this growing concern, VehicleSA has launched an innovative monthly fuel cost calculator, intended to assist consumers in making informed decisions.

Unlike traditional comparison tools that solely rely on theoretical fuel consumption figures, this new calculator takes into account real-time fuel prices and individual driving habits.

Consumers can plug in their desired mileage, revealing personalised estimates that allow them to consider fuel expenditure alongside other essential ownership costs, such as repayments and insurance.

This holistic approach reinforces the importance of understanding the true cost of vehicle ownership.

VehicleSA has also unveiled a comprehensive ranking system highlighting the "cheapest cars to run" across key vehicle segments, all based on an average monthly driving distance of 1,250 km at current fuel prices.

The data compellingly demonstrates variations in fuel costs even among similar models.

For instance, in the hatchback category, fuel expenses for the popular Toyota Vitz and Suzuki Celerio amount to approximately R1,398 monthly.

In striking contrast, the less efficient Renault Kwid can escalate to R1,631 monthly, a difference that can accumulate to more than R7,000 in savings annually for those who opt for the more fuel-efficient options.

A similar pattern emerges in the crossover segment.

The Renault Kiger stands out as one of the most affordable options to run, averaging around R1,664 monthly in fuel costs.

Conversely, larger or less efficient models can inflate fuel bills by over R300 per month.

Caradonna added, “Even within the same brand, moving up a model range can significantly increase your fuel spend.”

The launch of VehicleSA's tools may provide the crucial guidance needed to navigate this challenging landscape, highlighting that when it comes to car ownership, understanding fuel efficiency could lead to significant savings over time.

text:
In the spring of 2026, the global aviation industry is finding itself in the eye of a geopolitical storm. What began as localized tension in the Middle East has rippled across the planet, manifesting as a severe jet fuel crisis that is doing more than just delaying vacations. It is reshaping the way the world moves and, more critically, placing a stranglehold on the burgeoning economies of Africa.

As shipping routes through the strategic Strait of Hormuz face unprecedented threats, the “lifeblood” of international travel—Jet A1 fuel—has become a scarce and expensive commodity. For the average traveler, this means higher ticket prices; for African nations, it represents a looming economic catastrophe.

A World Interconnected by Risk

The current crisis underscores a terrifying reality: the world’s air travel infrastructure is incredibly vulnerable to supply shocks. Market analysts report that global shipments of jet fuel have plummeted to record lows. The reason is largely geographic. Nearly 41% of Europe’s aviation fuel is linked to oil that must pass through the Strait of Hormuz. When that artery is restricted, the heart of global travel skips a beat.

The immediate fallout has been a doubling of aviation fuel costs in just a few short months. This isn’t just a balance sheet issue for airlines; it’s a survival crisis. Major global carriers like Lufthansa have already been forced to axe thousands of flights. Icons of the sky, including British Airways and Virgin Atlantic, have had no choice but to pass these skyrocketing operational costs onto passengers through steep fare increases.

The New Face of Global Travel

For the everyday traveler, the “golden age” of cheap long-haul flights seems to be retreating into the distance. We are witnessing a fundamental shift in how people plan their journeys:

The Death of the “Spontaneous” Trip: With fares surging, travelers are abandoning last-minute getaways and long-haul intercontinental dreams.

Regionalism Over Globalism: There is a marked pivot toward short-haul and regional travel. People are staying closer to home, choosing destinations they can reach without crossing three time zones.

Hub-Centric Flying: Travelers are being forced to route through major international hubs, as airlines cut “secondary” or smaller routes to save on fuel, leaving smaller cities increasingly isolated.

Africa: The Epicenter of the Economic Shock

While a European or American traveler might grumble about an extra £200 on a ticket, for many African nations, the crisis is far more existential. Many African economies are heavily dependent on imported petroleum products. Unlike wealthier nations that can dip into strategic reserves or rely on domestic refining, much of Africa remains exposed to the raw volatility of the global market.

In Africa, the cost of jet fuel doesn’t just affect the wealthy flying to business meetings; it acts as an inflationary multiplier. When fuel prices rise, the cost of transporting food, essential medicines, and fertilizers rises with it. This deepens the financial strain on already fragile economies, pushing millions closer to the poverty line.

The Nigerian Perspective: A Domestic Struggle

Nigeria serves as a poignant case study for this crisis. The nation’s domestic aviation sector, already battling foreign exchange volatility and infrastructure deficits, is now at a breaking point.

Domestic carriers in Nigeria have issued stark warnings: the rising cost of Jet A1 fuel is no longer just a “challenge”—it is a threat to their continued existence. Local ticket prices have surged to levels that make air travel a luxury many average Nigerians can no longer afford. This isn’t just about holidays; it’s about the suspension of business travel that drives the economy, the disruption of family reunions, and the stalling of religious pilgrimages.

When the planes stop flying in a country as large as Nigeria, the gears of commerce begin to grind to a halt.

Is There a Silver Lining?

Experts agree that the world is unlikely to “run out” of fuel entirely. Supply chains are resilient, and alternative routes are being explored. However, the current crisis serves as a loud wake-up call for the industry to accelerate its transition away from a total reliance on traditional fossil fuels.

Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) and regional refining capabilities are no longer just “green” goals; they are now matters of national security and economic stability.

The Human Element

Beyond the data and the geopolitical maps, there is a human story. It’s the story of the small business owner in Lagos who can no longer afford to fly to meet suppliers. It’s the story of the family in London who has had to cancel a long-awaited reunion in Nairobi.

As we navigate the turbulence of 2026, the jet fuel crisis reminds us that in a globalized world, a conflict in one corner of the map can quiet the skies in another. The challenge for the coming years will be building a travel industry that isn’t just fast and far-reaching, but resilient enough to withstand the winds of political change.

title: Global Jet Fuel Crisis 2026: The Economic Turbulence Threatening African Skies and Global Trade
description:
A perfect storm of geopolitical shifts, refining bottlenecks, and logistics failures has birthed a global jet fuel (Jet A1) crisis that is doing far more than just delaying vacations.
It is reshaping the global travel landscape and, most urgently, threatening to derail the fragile economic progress of African nations.
When air travel becomes prohibitively expensive, the high-value supply chains—transporting electronics, fresh produce, and medical supplies—begin to snap.
Reshaping the Way We Move The 2026 crisis is forcing a fundamental rethink of global travel behavior.
The Bottom Line As we navigate the “empty skies” of 2026, it is clear that the jet fuel crisis is more than an industry problem; it is a global economic challenge.
text:
The year 2026 was supposed to be a hallmark for global connectivity, a time when the “new normal” of travel finally felt stable. Instead, the world’s aviation industry has hit a wall—or more accurately, a dry well. A perfect storm of geopolitical shifts, refining bottlenecks, and logistics failures has birthed a global jet fuel (Jet A1) crisis that is doing far more than just delaying vacations. It is reshaping the global travel landscape and, most urgently, threatening to derail the fragile economic progress of African nations.

From the bustling terminals of Heathrow to the strategic hubs in Lagos and Nairobi, the shortage is palpable. But while wealthier nations can often pivot or absorb costs, for many African economies, the inability to keep planes in the air is an existential threat.

The Global Ripple Effect

The crisis stems from a sharp decline in global refining capacity, coupled with disruptions in traditional oil supply routes through the Middle East. As Jet A1 stocks plummeted to decade lows earlier this year, the aviation industry saw an immediate, violent reaction.

Major international carriers have been forced to implement “fuel surcharges” that have sent ticket prices soaring by as much as 40% on long-haul routes. This isn’t just a headache for the luxury traveler; it is a direct blow to global commerce. When air travel becomes prohibitively expensive, the high-value supply chains—transporting electronics, fresh produce, and medical supplies—begin to snap.

Africa at the Epicenter

For Africa, the stakes are significantly higher. Aviation in Africa is not a luxury; it is a bridge. In a continent where road and rail infrastructure often lags behind, the “sky-highways” are what connect landlocked nations to global markets and regional neighbors to each other.

Nigeria as a Case Study:

The situation in Nigeria serves as a sobering warning for the rest of the continent. Despite being a major oil producer, the nation’s reliance on imported refined Jet A1 has left its domestic airlines vulnerable. Earlier this month, local ticket prices surged to unprecedented levels, making air travel a privilege reserved for the ultra-wealthy. When domestic flights stop, the internal gears of the continent’s largest economy begin to grind to a halt—affecting everything from the movement of agricultural goods to the flow of professional services.

Reshaping the Way We Move

The 2026 crisis is forcing a fundamental rethink of global travel behavior. We are seeing a “localization” of travel that hasn’t been witnessed in decades:

The Return of Regionalism: Travelers are increasingly opting for short-haul, regional trips that can be serviced by more fuel-efficient, smaller aircraft, abandoning long-haul “bucket list” journeys.

The Rise of Secondary Hubs: To save on fuel and airport fees, airlines are bypassing massive, expensive hubs in favor of smaller, more efficient regional airports.

The Digital Shift: As air travel costs become a significant line item on corporate balance sheets, we are seeing a resurgence in “virtual first” business culture, further dampening the demand for executive travel.

A Human Crisis in the Clouds

Beyond the macro-economic data lies a deeply human story. It’s the story of the small business owner in Rwanda who can no longer afford to fly to international trade fairs to find buyers for her textiles. It’s the story of families separated by thousands of miles who find their annual reunions priced out of reach.

Moreover, the high cost of fuel is slowing down the “humanitarian air bridge.” Relief organizations operating across the Sahel and Central Africa have reported that their operational costs have doubled, meaning less aid reaches those in desperate need because more of the budget is being swallowed by the fuel tank.

Is There a Way Out?

The 2026 crisis is a loud, uncomfortable wake-up call for the industry to move toward Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF)and more localized refining. African leaders are increasingly calling for “energy sovereignty”—the ability to refine aviation fuel on the continent rather than exporting crude only to buy back Jet A1 at a premium.

While the current turbulence is severe, it may eventually lead to a more resilient, localized, and green aviation sector. However, the transition period is proving to be a painful one.

The Bottom Line

As we navigate the “empty skies” of 2026, it is clear that the jet fuel crisis is more than an industry problem; it is a global economic challenge. For Africa, the goal is clear: build resilience or be left behind. The world is watching to see if the aviation industry can innovate its way out of this shortage before the economic damage becomes permanent.

Aviation is entering an era where fuel strategy, energy security, emissions exposure, and operational resilience are becoming inseparable.
The critical question is no longer whether SAF works; it is which pathway aligns with a nation’s real feedstock base, industrial capability, and long-term aviation demand curve.
Algae remains promising but operationally challenged due to contamination control, water intensity, biosecurity exposure, and open-culture bird attraction risks.

text: Sustainable Aviation Fuel can no longer be treated as a regulatory compliance exercise. Aviation is entering an era where fuel strategy, energy security, emissions exposure, and operational resilience are becoming inseparable. The industry today has seven recognised SAF pathways under ASTM certification frameworks HEFA, ATJ, FT-SPK, FT-SKA, CHJ, SIP, and PtL/e-SAF each with different maturity, feedstock, scalability, and lifecycle carbon profiles. The critical question is no longer whether SAF works; it is which pathway aligns with a nation’s real feedstock base, industrial capability, and long-term aviation demand curve. For India, the answer is increasingly clear. While HEFA remains the fastest near term solution, its feedstock ceiling limits strategic scalability. Algae remains promising but operationally challenged due to contamination control, water intensity, biosecurity exposure, and open-culture bird attraction risks. The most scalable and operationally aligned pathway for India through the 2030–2045 window is cellulosic ATJ and future FT-SPK built around agricultural residue. India’s advantage is not imported feedstock it is biomass already available in its fields. The nations and airlines that move beyond “minimum compliance” and build indigenous SAF ecosystems early will ultimately control not only carbon exposure, but long term fuel resilience, energy sovereignty, and strategic competitiveness.
